notes:
These notes cover John 7:27–53. I ran out of searches and page reads before I reached several sources: the NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey.org, the Orthodox and Pentecostal sites, and the full Matthew Henry text for verses 27–53. Those gaps are listed at the end. The commentators' church traditions shown in brackets come from me, not from the pages.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 27**
- **The crowd's belief.** Barnes says people expected the Messiah to be born in Bethlehem, but also believed he would be hidden or taken away in some mysterious manner, and appear again from some unexpected quarter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-27.htm
- **What they thought they knew.** Ellicott: the crowd knew Jesus as the carpenter's son and knew his family. They expected a Messiah who wouldn't live an ordinary life and whose immediate origin no one could know. He is the carpenter's son, and His mother, and brethren, and sisters, are well known (Matthew 13:55-56). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-27.htm
- **Parentage, not birthplace.** The Cambridge Bible says "whence" refers not to the Messiah's birthplace, which was known (John 7:41-42); nor to His remote descent... but to His parentage (John 6:42). The Pulpit Commentary agrees that birthplace wasn't the problem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-27.htm
- **Calvin [Reformed].** we are reminded how pernicious it is to mangle the Scriptures, and even Christ himself, so as not to admit more than the half of him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-27.html
- **Clarke [Methodist].** Had they considered his miraculous conception, they would have felt their minds relieved on this point. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-27.html
- **Matthew Henry.** The argument mixes two things. As for Christ's divine nature, it's true no one knows where he is from (Micah 5:2), but then the crowd didn't really know this man. As for his human nature, they did know his origins, but Scripture never said the Messiah's origin would be unknown. But then it is not true that as for this man they knew whence he was, for they knew not his divine nature, nor how the Word was made flesh. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_007.cfm
- **Guzik.** Many (but not all) of the Jews of that time believed the Messiah would appear suddenly, as if out of nowhere. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**v. 28**
- **Irony.** Guzik thinks Jesus' first sentence may well have been sarcastic. They thought they knew where He was from, but they were unaware of His heavenly origin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/
- **Ellicott.** Knowing someone's outward life tells little about who they really are. In the fullest sense, they neither knew Him nor from whence He came. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-28.html
- **Lenski [Lutheran].** Jesus' loud cry shows how deeply he was moved by the crowd's shallowness. His upbringing in Nazareth reveals nothing about his true origin and mission. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary
- **Even his earthly origin was misjudged.** The Biblical Illustrator says the crowd assumed Nazareth, but He was born at Bethlehem, and belonged to the tribe of Judah, and was of the lineage of David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-28.html
- **Two cries.** Jesus cries out twice at this feast: The first was the cry of rebuke (v. 28), the second was the cry of pity and compassion (Jn 7:37). https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_737_commentary

**v. 29**
- **Henry.** Christ did not run without sending, nor come as a private person, but with a public character. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_007.cfm
- **The real problem.** The crowd's real problem was spiritual blindness: they missed the Father who sent the Son. https://biblehub.com/john/7-27.htm

**v. 30**
- **God restrains them.** Jesus' claim to know God when they didn't angered his hearers, but God can tie men's hands, though he does not turn their hearts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-27.htm

**v. 31**
- **Guzik.** As Jesus spoke to the people, they were drawn to faith in Him. It didn't matter that many opposed Him or even wanted to kill Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**v. 32**
- **Guzik.** The officers wanted to arrest Jesus but couldn't. When they came back empty-handed, their leaders demanded to know why (see v. 46). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**vv. 33–34**
- **Henry.** Those who rejected the true Messiah were justly abandoned to a miserable and endless expectation of one that should never come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-27.html
- **Why they could not come.** A preacher quoted on Precept Austin gives three reasons: ignorance (they didn't know the Father), pride and unbelief. We cannot come to where Christ is, without possessing the Christ-like nature. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_737_commentary

**vv. 35–36:** I found no specific comment.

**v. 37**
- **The feast's water theme.** The Feast of Tabernacles recalled how God gave Israel water in the wilderness. Jesus boldly called people to Himself to drink and satisfy their deepest thirst, their spiritual thirst. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/
- **Timing and place.** Guzik says the saying mattered because of where Jesus said it (the temple courts) and when (the last day, after water had been poured out on the previous days). https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary
- **"Come to Me."** Precept Austin notes the invitation is to Jesus himself, not to a religion or ritual. "To Me" emphasizes that Jesus Alone is the Source of Soul Satisfying "water" of salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_737-39_commentary
- **Maclaren.** He adds the rock that gave water to John's list of Old Testament events Christ fulfils, alongside Jacob's ladder, the bronze serpent and the manna. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_737-39_commentary

**v. 38**
- **"As the Scripture has said."** Ellicott notes that the exact words are not found in any part of the Canonical Scriptures of the Old Testament. Westcott says the reference is to the general tenor of such passages as Isaiah 58:11;Zechariah 14:18, taken in connection with the original image Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Poole points to the Old Testament promises of the Spirit being poured out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-38.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-38.htm
- **"Belly."** Commentators take "belly" to mean the inner person. JFB: his inner man, his soul. Clarke: from his heart and soul; for in his soul shall this Spirit dwell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-38.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/john/7-38.html
- **Flowing out to others.** Ellicott says every one in living communion with Christ becomes himself the centre of spiritual influence. Barnes says real faith wants others to believe too. Gill [Baptist] says grace is of a diffusive and communicative nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-38.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-38.htm
- **Rivers, not a jar.** The Cambridge Bible notes that "rivers" comes first in the Greek, in marked contrast to the ewer of water poured each day during the Feast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-38.htm
- **Spurgeon [Baptist].** The work is inward and life-giving: It cannot come out of you if it is not in you: and it cannot be in you unless God the Holy Spirit places it there. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_738_commentary
- **Guzik.** It was not only a blessing received, but also becoming a source of blessing to others. He also links the saying to the prophecies of water flowing from Jerusalem, where the Messiah would reign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**v. 39**
- **Ryle [Anglican].** The Spirit was not yet poured out on believers in all His fullness, because our Lord had not yet finished His work. In a word, the dispensation of the Spirit had not yet begun. https://www.monergism.com/teaching-about-spirit-john-737-39
- **"Given" is supplied.** JFB, Ryle and Precept Austin all note that the word "given" is added by translators; the Greek literally says the Spirit "was not yet." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-39.htm and https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60727/
- **JFB.** The Spirit was a gift the communication of which was dependent upon His own departure to the Father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-39.htm
- **Same image, different Person.** in John 4 Living Water is a picture of Jesus and here in John 7 Living Water is a picture of the Holy Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_739_commentary

**vv. 40–41a**
- **Guzik.** Some said one thing, others said something else about who Jesus was; but everyone had an opinion. They could not be confronted with Jesus and remain truly neutral. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**vv. 41b–42**
- **Henry.** The crowd shows praiseworthy knowledge of Scripture. But they could have learned that Jesus was David's son and born in Bethlehem; but this they willingly are ignorant of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/john/7.htm
- **Constable.** Not only did they fail to perceive His heavenly origin, but they were also wrong about His earthly origin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-27.html

**v. 43**
- **Guzik.** The division didn't come because Jesus spoke foolishly, or because He spoke on a theologically controversial topic. He spoke about Himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**v. 44**
- **Guzik.** The arrest failed not because the officers were incompetent, It was because the time wasn't right yet in the Father's timing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/

**vv. 45–46**
- **Guzik.** The temple officers had heard many rabbis but had never heard anyone like Jesus. They found it impossible to do their assigned work of arresting and silencing Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/
- **A sermon quoted on Precept Austin.** John wants readers to hear the irony: Jesus speaks like no man because he is the Word made flesh. The guards, though, seem too afraid to stand with him. That is like people today who admire Jesus' wisdom but don't believe in him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary

**vv. 47–49:** I found no specific comment.

**vv. 50–52**
- **Nicodemus (Steven Cole).** His fair point brought a put-down. Cole adds that most commentators think his later help with Jesus' burial (19:38–40) shows he did finally believe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary
- **"From Galilee" (A. T. Robertson).** The jibe lumps Nicodemus in with the Galilean crowd. Robertson quotes Bernard: "These aristocrats of Jerusalem had a scornful contempt for the rural Galileans". https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-commentary

**v. 53**
- Enduring Word and Precept Austin both treat this verse as the start of the 7:53–8:11 passage (the woman caught in adultery). Precept Austin links an article titled "Does John 7:53-8:11 belong in the Bible?" I didn't read that article. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-7/ and https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-7-resources

## 2. Where interpreters differ

**v. 39: what "not yet given" means**
- **Gill [Baptist].** The apostles had already received the Spirit for new birth and holiness. At Pentecost they received a larger, even an extraordinary measure of his gifts and grace, to qualify them for greater work and service. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-39.htm
- **Ryle [Anglican].** He reads it as a new era: the Spirit's "dispensation" began after the ascension (see v. 39 above). https://www.monergism.com/teaching-about-spirit-john-737-39
- **An unnamed writer on Precept Austin.** Just as sinners receive Christ by faith for forgiveness, believers must in like manner receive Him by faith in order to be qualified for service. The same page also calls for "full surrender" to receive the Spirit's fullness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_739_commentary
- **Same page, another view.** The Spirit, who we receive when we trust the Lord Jesus as our Savior, empowers and refreshes us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_738_commentary
- I didn't read anything from the Pentecostal sites (ag.org, samstorms.org, pneumareview.com), so I can't report their view.

**vv. 37–38: whose "belly"?**
- Some join the first words of v. 38 to v. 37 ("let him that believeth on Me drink"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-38.htm
- The *Wells of Living Water* commentary capitalises "His" because it is from Christ, primarily, that the Living Waters flow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lwc/john-7.html
- Most of the commentators above read it as the believer's inner self.

## 3. Other views

- **Augustine (Catholic/Church Father), v. 38.** There is therefore an inner thirst and an inner belly, because there is an inner man. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701032.htm
- **Augustine, v. 39.** The Spirit had worked before, but a new way of giving was coming. For nowhere do we read before this, that men being gathered together had, by receiving the Holy Ghost, spoken in the tongues of all nations. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701032.htm
- **Chrysostom (quoted in the Biblical Illustrator), v. 38.** The rivers show grace that never runs out, seen in The wisdom of Stephen, the tongue of Peter, the strength of Paul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/7-38.html
- **Jewish background (from older commentaries).** These cite rabbinic and early sayings about a hidden Messiah. The Pulpit Commentary quotes Justin Martyr's Trypho saying Christ is unknown, and does not even know himself, and has no power until Elias come to anoint him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/7-27.htm

**Not found:** NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or catholic.com pages, Lutheran site material beyond Lenski, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Verses 35–36 and 47–49 have no notes.
